theme: Sky and Earth as a pair (West 2007 ch. 4)

plan.english: Father Sky, Mother Broad One, hear us!

notes: The vocative pair of RV 6.51.5 (dyaùḥ pítar, pŕ̥thivi mā́tar); Ζεῦ πάτερ in prayer; Latin Iu(p)piter is the univerbated vocative *dyéw ph₂ter. 'The Broad One' is *pl̥th₂wih₂, the feminine of pléth₂us used as Earth's name: Ved. pr̥thivī́ and OE Folde, which the ploughing charm addresses as mother ('Folde, fīra mōdor'). Interpolated: ḱlew- 'hear' (aorist imperative dual, cf. śr̥ṇutam in RV 1.89.4, a Dyaus–Pr̥thivī stanza, though there addressed to the Aśvins) and enclitic nos 'us' (Ved. naḥ in 6.51.5b). Ved. ádhruk 'guileless' has no cognate in the other branches and is left out.

theme: Sky and Earth as a pair (West 2007 ch. 4)

plan.english: Sky is our father, and the Broad One is our mother.

notes: Vedic pairs Dyaus 'father' with Pr̥thivī 'mother' (RV 1.89.4; 1.164.33 dyaúr me pitā́ ... mātā́ pr̥thivī́; AV Paipp. 5.21.1 Dyáuś ca naḥ pitā́ Pr̥thivī́ ca mātā́). Latin: Varro's 'Iuppiter pater ..., Tellus mater' (West doubts its antiquity) and Lucretius' pater aether / mater terra; OE Folde (= pr̥thivī́) is 'mother'. Interpolated: the copula (the Vedic is a nominal sentence) and nos 'our' (AV Paipp. naḥ, RV me: Indo-Iranian only).

Ved. mahé pitré divé 'for great Father Heaven' (RV 1.71.5) and máh- of Dyaus (3.54.2, 1.22.13); Homer has Ζεῦ πάτερ ... μέγιστε (Il. 3.276) and Διὸς μεγάλου (Il. 2.134 and often). The dative of the honoured god follows the Vedic. Interpolated: the verb h₁erkʷ- 'praise, sing' (Ved. arca, RV 3.54.2: Indo-Iranian only), 1st sg.

plan.english: The rain-clouds of Sky rain upon the earth.

notes: Homeric Διὸς ὄμβρος 'Zeus' rain' = Vedic divó vr̥ṣṭí- 'Dyaus' rain'; the Vedic cognate of ὄμβρος, abhrá- 'rain-cloud', stands beside diváḥ in RV 5.84.3 (a hymn to Earth), and Latin imber, also from *n̥bʰ-r-, is the rain that father aether casts into mother earth (Lucr. 1.250f.). Interpolated: the verb h₂wers- 'rain' (Ved. várṣanti; the engine has only the aorist of the root, so a gnomic aorist) and 'upon the earth' (Ved. kṣmayā́, instrumental, in the same stanza), rendered as a locative.

plan.english: The immortals made the two eyes of Sky.

notes: Ved. divó ... akṣī́ 'the two eyes of Heaven' (sun and moon, RV 1.72.10) corresponds etymologically, dual for dual, to Homeric Διὸς ὄσσε (Il. 14.286); West 2007 ch. 4 n. 25. Interpolated (Vedic only): the subject amŕ̥tāḥ 'the immortals' and the verb, the imperfect of the nasal present kʷr̥néw- (Ved. ákr̥ṇvan).

plan.english: You hold the earth and the clouds.

notes: Hittite to Wašezzili 'you hold heaven and earth' (KUB 8.41 ii 6′; again to the Storm-god ii 12′); Zarathushtra 'who holds the earth below and the heavens (nabā̊) from falling?' (Y. 44.4). PIE *nébʰos 'cloud' is the word for 'sky' in Hittite nēpis and Avestan nabah-; the English keeps the PIE gloss. Interpolated: the verb, Indo-Iranian *dʰer- 'hold' (Av. dərətā, Ved. dādhā́ra; here the causative present, Ved. dhāráyati), since Hittite uses ḫark-; 2nd sg pro-drop after the Hittite.

plan.english: The earth is a broad seat for the gods.

notes: Heaven and Earth are urvī́ sádmanī 'the two broad seats' (RV 1.185.6); Earth is ἕδος ἀσφαλές of the immortals (Hes. Th. 117f.) and εὐρυεδὴς χθών 'broad-seated earth' (Simonides); kṣā́m ... urvī́m = εὐρεῖα χθών. Ved. sádman- (*sed-mn̥) and Gk ἕδος (*sédos, = Ved. sádas-) are the same root. 'For the gods' is interpolated: Ved. devā́nām and Gk ἀθανάτων are different words.

εὐρεῖα χθών = Ved. kṣā́m ... urvī́m (West 2007 ch. 4, 'Attributes of Earth'); the Greek earth 'nourishes' (τρέφει, Il. 11.741). The verb and object come from the Gathic 'this earth that bears us' (Y. 38.1 imąm ... ząm ... yā nā̊ baraitī): bʰer- and nos are Indo-Iranian only, so interpolated.

plan.english: The stars are the ornament of the heaven.

notes: The heaven that Mazdā wears is stəhr-paēsah- 'star-ornamented' (Yt. 13.2–3; Av. paēsah- = *péyḱos exactly); Agni 'adorned the vault with stars' (RV 1.68.10, Ved. piś-); Euripides' ἀστέρων ποικίλματα (Hel. 1096, cited from West 2007 ch. 9) has the same root (cf. ποικίλον ἀστερόεντα, Il. 16.134, of a breastplate). 'Heaven' is h₂éḱmō (Av. asman- 'heaven', Ved. áśman- 'stone'): Iranian only, interpolated; copula interpolated.

The Aśvins are Divó nápātā 'grandsons/offspring of Dyaus' (RV 1.117.12, 1.182.1, 4.44.2, 10.61.4), the Dioskouroi the 'youths of Zeus'; only the genitive of *Dyeus is shared (Gk κοῦροι is another word, and Lithuanian Diẽvo sūnẽliai has *deywós). Interpolated: népōts (Vedic only; Latin 'Iouis nepotes' is West's illustration, not an attestation) and gʷem- 'come' (Ved. ā́ gatam, aorist imperative dual).

plan.english: Sky is the father, the begetter of the gods.

notes: Ved. dyaúḥ pitā́ janitā́ 'Dyaus the father, the begetter' (RV 4.1.10; 1.164.33), and Heaven and Earth are devā́nām ... jánitrī 'begetters of the gods' (1.185.6); Catullus calls Iupiter (< *dyew-ph₂ter) diuum genitor (64.26f.). Greek πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε (Il. 1.544) is the same idea in other words. Interpolated: the copula.

plan.english: Father Sky has cast me forth to you.

notes: The divine messenger's credential: Iris 'Father Zeus sent me forth to tell you this' (Il. 11.201), Mercury 'my father (Jupiter) sent me here to you' (Plaut. Amph. 19f.). Shared: *Dyeus and *ph₂tḗr, and the 1st sg pronoun (με, me). The verb follows the Greek: προ-έ-ηκε is pró + the k-aorist of *Hyeh₁- 'throw, cast' (ἵημι 'let go, send'); the English keeps the lexicon's sense. Latin misit is another root, so the verb is interpolated.

theme: Sky and Earth as a pair (West 2007 ch. 4)

plan.english: I ask Sky and the Broad One, the Mother.

notes: The ploughman's prayer to Sky and Earth: Hesiod 'pray to Zeus of the Earth and pure Demeter' at the first ploughing (Op. 465); Cato's farmer 'Iupiter, ... bonas preces precor' (Agr. 134.3); the OE field charm prays to 'earth and heaven above' and hails 'Folde, mother of men'. *meh₂tḗr stands in Δη-μήτηρ and mōdor, *pl̥th₂wih₂ in folde and pr̥thivī́ (RV 3.54.2, praise of Heaven and Earth). Interpolated: the verb, the -sḱé- present of *preḱ- 'ask' (Latin precor has the root; Greek εὔχεσθαι and OE biddan are other words).

plan.english: The daughter of Sky is born.

notes: Divó duhitā́ 'daughter of Dyaus' is uniquely Uṣas's title (over thirty times; 'at whose yoking the daughter of Dyaus is born', RV 10.39.12); Greek Διὸς θυγάτηρ is used of Helen (Od. 4.227), Aphrodite and the Muse; Lithuanian Diẽvo dukrýtė (of the Sun) has *deywós, so only dʰugh₂tḗr is shared there. Interpolated: the present middle of ǵenh₁- 'be born' (Ved. jā́yate; Gk γίγνομαι is the reduplicated present used here).
